title: Which set does this address land in

prereqs.why: The whole problem is the offset/index/tag split, and the field widths come from the geometry.
Each field is one shift and one mask, and the masks come from the sizes being powers of two.
The offset field exists because a cache moves whole blocks, not single bytes.

statement:
Given a cache's geometry, decode addresses into the three fields the hardware
uses to look them up.

Input, all on the first lines: `cacheBytes assoc blockBytes addrBits q`, then
`q` addresses in decimal. `cacheBytes`, `assoc` and `blockBytes` are powers of
two; `assoc` is the number of ways per set.

Print the derived geometry, then one line per address, then how many **adjacent
pairs** of addresses in the input land in the same set:

```
geometry sets <S> offsetbits <ob> indexbits <ib> tagbits <tb>
<address> offset <o> index <i> tag <t>
...
sameset <count>
```

```
input:   32768 8 64 48 3        output:  geometry sets 64 offsetbits 6 indexbits 6 tagbits 36
         0                               0 offset 0 index 0 tag 0
         64                              64 offset 0 index 1 tag 0
         4096                            4096 offset 0 index 0 tag 1
                                         sameset 0
```

That is a 32 KiB 8-way cache with 64-byte lines - a realistic L1 data cache.

### How the address is split

A cache holds whole **blocks**, arranged in **sets**, with `assoc` blocks in each
set. So an address has to answer three questions, and each is a slice of its
bits:

```
    +--------------------------+------------+-------------+
    |           tag            |   index    |   offset    |
    +--------------------------+------------+-------------+
      which block, among all      which       which byte
      that map to this set         set         in the block

     offsetBits = log2(blockBytes)
     indexBits  = log2(sets),  where sets = cacheBytes / (assoc * blockBytes)
     tagBits    = addrBits - indexBits - offsetBits
```

The **low** bits are the offset, because consecutive addresses are in the same
block - which is the entire point of fetching a block at a time. The **middle**
bits are the index, so addresses that are near each other spread across
different sets instead of fighting over one. The tag is everything left over,
and it is stored in the cache next to the data so a lookup can tell which of the
many blocks that map to a set is actually present.

### Extracting a field

```cpp
offset = addr & (blockBytes - 1);
index  = (addr >> offsetBits) & (sets - 1);
tag    = addr >> (offsetBits + indexBits);
```

`blockBytes - 1` is a mask of `offsetBits` ones, because `blockBytes` is a power
of two - `64 - 1` is `0b111111`. That is the only reason cache dimensions are
always powers of two: it makes the division free.

### Boundary cases

A fully associative cache, where `sets` is 1, `indexBits` is 0, and there is no
index field at all - the mask `sets - 1` is then 0, which must still work. A
direct-mapped cache, where `assoc` is 1. A block size of 1 byte, so `offsetBits`
is 0. The address 0. The largest address the bit width allows. Addresses exactly
one block apart and exactly one *way size* apart, which is how a conflict is
constructed.

### Platform assumptions

Addresses are unsigned and fit in `addrBits` bits, with `addrBits` between 1 and
48 - so `std::uint64_t` holds every value and every intermediate with room to
spare. `cacheBytes`, `assoc` and `blockBytes` are powers of two, and
`assoc * blockBytes` divides `cacheBytes` exactly, so the number of sets is a
whole power of two and no rounding is involved. Shift amounts are always less
than 64, which matters because shifting by the width of the type or more is
undefined behaviour.
hints: Work out the three widths first: `offsetBits = log2(blockBytes)`, `sets = cacheBytes / (assoc * blockBytes)`, `indexBits = log2(sets)`, and `tagBits` is whatever remains of `addrBits`. A small loop that counts how many times you can halve a value is all the log2 you need.
Masks from powers of two: a mask of k ones is `(1 << k) - 1`, and since `blockBytes` is already `1 << offsetBits`, the offset mask is just `blockBytes - 1`. Same for the index mask and `sets`.

A fully associative cache has `sets == 1`, so `indexBits` is 0 and the index mask `sets - 1` is 0 - meaning `(addr >> 0) & 0` is always 0. That is correct, not a special case: with one set, every address is in set 0.

templates.python:
import sys

def log2exact(v):
    k = 0
    while v > 1:
        v >>= 1
        k += 1
    return k

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    if not data:
        return
    pos = 0
    cache_bytes = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    assoc = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    block_bytes = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    addr_bits = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    q = int(data[pos]); pos += 1

    # sets, offset_bits, index_bits, tag_bits, then the per-address fields

main()
